q:
Had I learnt acting as a child, I__________a famous film star.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
'Had I learnt …' is an inverted third conditional (= 'If I had learnt …'), an unreal condition in the past. The main clause of a third conditional takes would/could/might + have + past participle → 'I could have been a famous film star'. 'will be', 'can be', 'am going to be' are real/future forms and clash with a past-unreal condition.
Trap: Spot the inverted conditional: 'Had I …', 'Were I …', 'Should you …' = 'If …'. Match the condition type: past perfect in the if-clause ⇒ 'would/could have + V3' in the result clause.

q:
Rafi told Mary, "I am thinking of watching a film this weekend."
The following reports the above statement in indirect speech:
Rafi told Mary that he _________ of watching a film that weekend.
solution:
Direct → indirect speech with a past reporting verb ('told') back-shifts the tense: present continuous 'am thinking' → past continuous 'was thinking'; 'I' → 'he'; 'this weekend' → 'that weekend'. So 'he was thinking of watching a film that weekend'.
Trap: Options keep one wrong piece each: 'is thinking' (no back-shift), 'am thinking' (no pronoun/tense change), 'thought' (wrong aspect — continuous must stay continuous).

q:
Ravi had __________ younger brother who taught at __________ university. He was widely regarded as _________ honorable man.
Select the option with the correct sequence of articles to fill in the blanks.
solution:
Choose by the first SOUND, not letter. 'younger' — consonant sound → a younger brother (non-specific, first mention). 'university' starts with the sound /juː/ (a consonant 'y' sound) → a university. 'honorable' starts with a silent h → vowel sound /ɒ/ → an honorable man. Sequence a; a; an.
Trap: 'an university' looks right by spelling but is wrong by sound; 'a honorable' is the mirror trap (silent h). Words like European, one, unique take 'a'; hour, honest, heir take 'an'.

q: 'People are crowding around ____ pit into which ____ elephant has fallen. I have never seen an elephant looking more bewildered ____ miserable. Here it is in a most undignified position, thrust into a pit and made to look up ____ a vast, curiosity-stricken crowd.' Choose the option with the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks.
solution:
Blank 1: first mention of a singular countable noun beginning with a consonant sound → 'a pit'. Blank 2: 'elephant' starts with a vowel sound → 'an elephant'. Blank 3 joins two adjectives in a comparison → 'more bewildered and miserable'. Blank 4: the phrasal verb is 'look up at' someone. So a; an; and; at.
Trap: Mixed article + conjunction + preposition blanks: fill the blanks you are sure of first (here 'an elephant' and 'look up at') and eliminate — only B fits both.
source: GATE 2026 ME · Q6 (also CE Set 2 Q6)

q: We reached the station late, and ___________ missed the train.
solution:
The adverb must modify the verb 'missed' and mean 'almost': nearly missed = almost missed. 'near' is an adjective/preposition, not the adverb of degree; 'utterly'/'mostly' do not give the sense of 'almost (but not quite)'.
Trap: Adjective vs adverb: 'near' (adjective) vs 'nearly' (adverb = almost). 'We were late, and nearly missed the train' — the lateness almost caused it.

q: Gauri said that she can play keyboard _______ her sister.
solution:
Comparison of equality uses as + adverb (positive degree) + as. The verb 'play' needs an adverb: 'as well as her sister'. 'worse', 'better', 'nicest' are comparative/superlative forms and cannot sit inside 'as … as'.
Trap: 'as better as' / 'as nicest as' mix two degrees of comparison — never correct. Also 'well' (adverb) not 'good' after an action verb.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
Steve was advised to keep his head _____ (i) _____ before heading _____ (ii) _____ to bat; for, while he had a head _____ (iii) _____ batting, he could only do so with a cool head _____ (iv) _____ his shoulders.
solution:
Fixed idioms with 'head': keep one's head down (stay focused, avoid distraction); head out (go out — here, out to bat); have a head for something (have a talent for it); a cool head on one's shoulders (calm, sensible). So (i) down (ii) out (iii) for (iv) on.
Trap: Four similar-looking prepositions; anchor on the fixed phrase you know best ('head on his shoulders' → on) and eliminate. Only C has both 'out' for (ii) and 'on' for (iv).

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)–(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
Following a row ____(i) ______ the shopkeeper ____(ii) ______ the price of a frying pan, the cook stood ____(iii) ______ a row to withdraw cash _____(iv) ______ the ATM booth.
solution:
'a row (quarrel) with someone over something' → row with the shopkeeper over the price; 'stood in a row (line)'; withdraw cash at the ATM booth (a point location). So with; over; in; at.
Trap: 'row' is used in two senses (quarrel /raʊ/ and line /rəʊ/) — each takes a different preposition. 'at' for a specific point (at the ATM, at the station).

q: Mr. X speaks ____________ Japanese ___________ Chinese.
solution:
Paired (correlative) conjunctions must match: neither … nor (negative: not this and not that), either … or (positive choice). 'neither … or' and 'either … nor' are mismatched pairs; 'also … but' is not a correlative pair. So 'Mr. X speaks neither Japanese nor Chinese'.
Trap: Correlative pairs: either/or, neither/nor, both/and, not only/but also, whether/or. Never mix halves.

q: 'The team ____ more than 300 runs in 20 overs ____ rains. However, some players needed to improve their batting skills.' Choose the option with the correct sequence of words to fill the blanks.
solution:
Blank 1 needs a finite verb in the past (the second sentence is in the past: 'needed') → scored. 'scoring' is a participle and leaves the sentence without a main verb; 'score' is the wrong tense. Blank 2 needs a preposition of concession followed by a noun → despite rains ('in spite of' is also correct, but it comes paired with 'scoring' in D, which fails blank 1).
Trap: 'despite' never takes 'of' ('despite of' is wrong); 'in spite of' always does. Check each option as a pair — one wrong half kills the option.
source: GATE 2026 ME · Q1 (also CE Set 2 Q1)

q: The President, along with the Council of Ministers, _________to visit India next week. Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
The subject is 'The President' (singular). Phrases introduced by along with, together with, as well as, accompanied by, in addition to do NOT change the number of the subject. Singular subject + simple present for a planned intention → 'The President … wishes to visit India next week'.
Trap: The plural noun 'Ministers' sitting next to the blank tempts 'wish'. Cover the 'along with …' phrase and read 'The President ____ to visit'.

q:
In the given text, the blanks are numbered (i)-(iv). Select the best match for all the blanks.
From the ancient Athenian arena to the modern Olympic stadiums, athletics ___(i)___ the potential for a spectacle. The crowd ___(ii)___ with bated breath as the Olympian artist twists his body, stretching the javelin behind him. Twelve strides in, he begins to cross-step. Six cross-steps ___(iii)___ in an abrupt stop on his left foot. As his body ___(iv)___ like a door turning on a hinge, the javelin is launched skyward at a precise angle.
solution:
(i) 'athletics' is a singular field of study/sport → athletics holds. (ii) 'The crowd' is a collective noun acting as one unit → the crowd waits. (iii) 'Six cross-steps' is plural → culminate. (iv) 'his body' is singular → pivots. Only D gives holds/waits/culminate/pivots.
Trap: Nouns ending in -s that are singular (athletics, physics, news, mathematics); collective nouns (crowd, team, committee) take singular verbs when acting as one unit.

q: Identify the grammatically correct sentence:
options: It is I who am responsible for this fiasco.
It is myself who is responsible for this fiasco.
It is I who is responsible for this fiasco.
It is I who are responsible for this fiasco.
solution:
In 'It is I who …', the relative pronoun 'who' takes the person and number of its antecedent 'I' (first person singular), so the verb is am: 'It is I who am responsible'. 'myself' cannot be the complement here (a reflexive needs a matching subject), and 'is'/'are' do not agree with 'I'.
Trap: 'It is I who is …' sounds natural in speech but is the classic GATE trap — the verb after 'who' agrees with the antecedent, not with 'it'.

subtopic: other parts of speech (pronouns, sentence parts)
q:
'The shopkeeper sells lemons.'
In this sentence, the word 'lemons' is the
solution:
'The shopkeeper (subject) sells (verb) lemons (object).' The noun that receives the action of a transitive verb is its object; the predicate is the whole 'sells lemons', not the single word 'lemons'.
Trap: Predicate = verb + everything after it; object = the noun receiving the action.
source: GATE 2026 EE · Q1 (also CE Set 1 Q1)

subtopic: other parts of speech (pronouns, sentence parts)
q: The people ____ were at the demonstration were from all sections of society.
solution:
The blank refers back to 'the people' (persons) and is the SUBJECT of 'were at the demonstration' → subject relative pronoun for persons = who. 'whom' is the object form, 'whose' is possessive, 'which' is for things.
Trap: Test: replace with he/him — 'they were at the demonstration' (subject → who), never 'them were'.

subtopic: other parts of speech (pronouns, sentence parts)
q:
Consider the following sentences:
(i) Everybody in the class is prepared for the exam.
(ii) Babu invited Danish to his home because he enjoys playing chess.
Which of the following is the CORRECT observation about the above two sentences?
options: (i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is unambiguous
(i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is ambiguous
(i) is grammatically incorrect and (ii) is ambiguous
(i) is grammatically correct and (ii) is unambiguous
solution:
(i) 'Everybody' is grammatically singular → 'is prepared' is correct. (ii) 'he' (and 'his') could refer to Babu or to Danish — the pronoun's antecedent is unclear, so the sentence is ambiguous. Hence (i) correct, (ii) ambiguous.
Trap: Indefinite pronouns everybody/everyone/each/nobody take singular verbs; a pronoun with two possible male antecedents creates ambiguity.

subtopic: word meaning, confusable words, intensity analogies
q: The ___________ is too high for it to be considered __________.
solution:
'fare' = the price of a ticket/journey (noun); 'fair' = just, reasonable (adjective). 'The fare is too high for it to be considered fair.' ('faer' is not a word.)
Trap: Homophones: identify part of speech needed in each blank — noun (fare) then adjective (fair).

subtopic: word meaning, confusable words, intensity analogies
q: "I cannot support this proposal. My __________ will not permit it."
solution:
conscience = the inner sense of right and wrong; 'My conscience will not permit it' fits refusing to support a proposal. 'conscious' (adjective: aware), 'consensus' (general agreement), 'consent' (permission) do not fit 'My ____ will not permit it'.
Trap: Look-alike words (conscience/conscious/consensus/consent): the blank after 'My' needs a noun that can 'permit'.

subtopic: word meaning, confusable words, intensity analogies
q:
The CEO's decision to downsize the workforce was considered myopic– because it sacrificed long-term stability to accommodate short-term gains.
Select the most appropriate option that can replace the word "myopic" without changing the meaning of the sentence.
solution:
'myopic' literally means short-sighted; figuratively, lacking foresight — here, sacrificing long-term stability for short-term gains. Replacement: shortsighted. 'visionary', 'progressive', 'innovative' are near-opposites.
Trap: Context clue 'long-term stability … short-term gains' already tells you the meaning even if the word is unfamiliar.

subtopic: word meaning, confusable words, intensity analogies
q:
Match the words in the first column with their synonyms in the second column.
(i) Lonely (ii) Literal (iii) Lousy (iv) Lethal
(p) Verbatim (q) Solitary (r) Deadly (s) Terrible
solution:
Lonely ≈ Solitary (q); Literal ≈ Verbatim — word for word (p); Lousy ≈ Terrible — very bad (s); Lethal ≈ Deadly (r). So (i)-(q); (ii)-(p); (iii)-(s); (iv)-(r).
Trap: Fix the certain pairs first (Lethal–Deadly, Lonely–Solitary); only option A keeps both.
source: GATE 2026 EE · Q6 (also CE Set 1 Q6)

subtopic: word meaning, confusable words, intensity analogies
q: If ‘→’ denotes increasing order of intensity, then the meaning of the words [charm → enamor → bewitch] is analogous to [bored → _______ → weary]. Which one of the given options is appropriate to fill the blank?
solution:
[charm → enamor → bewitch] increase in intensity of attraction. Analogously [bored → jaded → weary]: jaded = tired and bored from having had too much of something — between 'bored' and 'weary'. 'baffled' (confused), 'dead', 'worsted' (defeated) are not on the boredom/fatigue scale.
Trap: Intensity-ladder analogies (a GATE 2024 favourite): the missing word must be on the SAME meaning scale and between its neighbours.

q: The movie was funny and I ____________.
solution:
Idiom: can't/couldn't help + V-ing = cannot stop oneself from doing something. 'The movie was funny and I couldn't help laughing.' After 'help' in this idiom the verb is a gerund (-ing), never a past form.
Trap: 'couldn't help laughed' — wrong verb form; 'could help laughing' reverses the meaning.

q:
Even though I had planned to go skiing with my friends, I had to __________ at the last moment because of an injury.
Select the most appropriate option to complete the above sentence.
solution:
Phrasal verb back out = withdraw from something already agreed/planned. 'I had to back out at the last moment because of an injury.' 'back up' = support / make a copy; 'back of', 'back on' are not the needed phrasal verb.
Trap: Phrasal verbs change meaning with the particle: back out (withdraw), back up (support), back down (concede).

subtopic: Reading comprehension / inference from a passage
q:
In a recently conducted national entrance test, boys constituted 65% of those who appeared for the test. Girls constituted the remaining candidates and they accounted for 60% of the qualified candidates.
Which one of the following is the correct logical inference based on the information provided in the above passage?
options: Equal number of boys and girls qualified
Equal number of boys and girls appeared for the test
The number of boys who appeared for the test is less than the number of girls who appeared
The number of boys who qualified the test is less than the number of girls who qualified
solution:
Let N candidates appear: boys 0.65N, girls 0.35N. Of the Q qualified, girls = 0.6Q and boys = 0.4Q. So fewer boys than girls qualified (0.4Q < 0.6Q) — option D. A is false (0.4Q ≠ 0.6Q); B and C contradict 65% boys appearing.
Trap: Don't confuse the two bases: 65% is of those who APPEARED, 60% is of those who QUALIFIED. Only conclusions about the same base can be compared directly.

subtopic: Reading comprehension / inference from a passage
q:
A survey for a certain year found that 90% of pregnant women received medical care at least once before giving birth. Of these women, 60% received medical care from doctors, while 40% received medical care from other healthcare providers.
Given this information, which one of the following statements can be inferred with certainty?
options: More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor.
Less than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor.
More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at most once from a doctor.
Less than half of the pregnant women received medical care at most once from a doctor.
solution:
90% received care at least once; 60% of THESE got it from doctors → 0.9 × 0.6 = 54% of all pregnant women received care from a doctor at least once → more than half. Option A.
Trap: Percent of a percent: multiply the bases (0.9 × 0.6). B/C/D invent 'at most once' or reverse the inequality.

subtopic: Reading comprehension / inference from a passage
q: Based only on the conversation below, identify the logically correct inference: "Even if I had known that you were in the hospital, I would not have gone there to see you", Ramya told Josephine.
options: Ramya knew that Josephine was in the hospital.
Ramya did not know that Josephine was in the hospital.
Ramya and Josephine were once close friends; but now, they are not.
Josephine was in the hospital due to an injury to her leg.
solution:
'Even if I had known …' is a third-conditional (counterfactual) clause: it talks about an unreal past condition, which tells us that in reality Ramya did not know Josephine was in the hospital. Nothing in the sentence supports the friendship story (C) or the cause of hospitalisation (D).
Trap: Counterfactuals ('If I had known …') imply the opposite of the condition actually happened. Reject options that add outside information.

subtopic: Reading comprehension / inference from a passage
q:
A recent survey shows that 65% of tobacco users were advised to stop consuming tobacco. The survey also shows that 3 out of 10 tobacco users attempted to stop using tobacco.
Based only on the information in the above passage, which one of the following options can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco made an attempt to do so.
A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco did not attempt to do so.
Approximately 30% of tobacco users successfully stopped consuming tobacco.
Approximately 65% of tobacco users successfully stopped consuming tobacco.
solution:
65% were advised to stop; only 30% (3 in 10) of ALL users attempted to stop. Even if every attempter was among the advised, at most 30 of the 65 advised attempted, so at least 35 of 65 (≈54%) of the advised did not attempt → 'a majority of those advised did not attempt' is certain (B). Attempting ≠ succeeding, so C and D cannot be inferred.
Trap: 'Attempted' vs 'successfully stopped' — inference questions punish answers that upgrade the claim. Use the worst-case overlap to test 'certain' statements.

subtopic: Reading comprehension / inference from a passage
q: "His life was divided between the books, his friends, and long walks. A solitary man, he worked at all hours without much method, and probably courted his fatal illness in this way. To his own name there is not much to show; but such was his liberality that he was continually helping others, and fruits of his erudition are widely scattered, and have gone to increase many a comparative stranger's reputation." (From E.V. Lucas's 'A Funeral') Based only on the information provided in the above passage, which one of the following statements is true?
options: The solitary man described in the passage is dead.
Strangers helped create a grand reputation for the solitary man described in the passage.
The solitary man described in the passage found joy in scattering fruits.
The solitary man worked in a court where he fell ill.
solution:
'probably courted his fatal illness' — a fatal illness, in a piece titled 'A Funeral', with everything in the past tense → the man is dead (A). B reverses who helped whom (he increased strangers' reputations); C misreads the metaphor 'fruits of his erudition'; D misreads 'courted' (invited) as a law court.
Trap: Literal-vs-figurative traps: 'courted' (invited), 'fruits' (results). The correct option is usually a modest, directly supported statement.

q:
Sequence the following sentences in a coherent passage.
P: This fortuitous geological event generated a colossal amount of energy and heat that resulted in the rocks rising to an average height of 4 km across the contact zone.
Q: Thus, the geophysicists tend to think of the Himalayas as an active geological event rather than as a static geological feature.
R: The natural process of the cooling of this massive edifice absorbed large quantities of atmospheric carbon dioxide, altering the earth’s atmosphere and making it better suited for life.
S: Many millennia ago, a breakaway chunk of bedrock from the Antarctic Plate collided with the massive Eurasian Plate.
solution:
S (Many millennia ago … a chunk of the Antarctic Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate) — sets the scene with a time marker → P ('This fortuitous geological event' refers to the collision) → R ('this massive edifice' = the risen rocks; its cooling) → Q ('Thus, geophysicists …' — conclusion). SPRQ.
Trap: Demonstratives ('This event', 'this massive edifice') must come after the noun they point to; 'Thus' signals the concluding sentence.

q:
Identify the option that has the most appropriate sequence such that a coherent paragraph is formed:
P. At once, without thinking much, people rushed towards the city in hordes with the sole aim of grabbing as much gold as they could.
Q. However, little did they realize about the impending hardships they would have to face on their way to the city: miles of mud, unfriendly forests, hungry beasts and inimical local lords - all of which would reduce their chances of getting gold to almost zero.
R. All of them thought that easily they could lay their hands on gold and become wealthy overnight.
S. About a hundred years ago, the news that gold had been discovered in Kolar spread like wildfire and the whole State was in raptures.
solution:
S (news that gold was discovered in Kolar spread) → P ('At once … people rushed towards the city') → R ('All of them thought …' — their motive) → Q ('However, little did they realize …' — the contrasting outcome). S→P→R→Q.
Trap: Time marker 'About a hundred years ago' opens; 'However' introduces the twist and usually comes last or after the idea it contrasts.

q: The number of minutes spent by two students, X and Y, exercising every day in a given week are shown in the bar chart (horizontal bars, one pair per day). The number of days in the given week in which one of the students spent a minimum of 10% more than the other student, on a given day, is
solution:
Compare larger/smaller each day: Sun 65/55 = 1.18; Sat 60/50 = 1.20; Fri 35/20 = 1.75; Thu 60/55 = 1.09 (< 1.10); Wed 60/50 = 1.20; Tue 65/55 = 1.18; Mon 70/45 = 1.56. Six days have at least 10% more → 6.
Trap: '10% more than the other' is measured on the SMALLER value: 55 → 60 is only 9.1% more. Thursday is the planted near-miss.

q: The number of students passing or failing in an exam for a particular subject are presented in the bar chart. Students who pass the exam cannot appear for the exam again. Students who fail the exam in the first attempt must appear for the exam in the following year. Students always pass the exam in their second attempt. The numbers of students who took the exam for the first time in the year 2 and the year 3 respectively, are ____.
solution:
Everyone who appears in a year = pass + fail. Year 2 appeared = 60 + 5 = 65, of whom the 10 who failed in year 1 are repeaters (they all pass) → first-timers = 65 − 10 = 55. Year 3 appeared = 50 + 3 = 53, repeaters = 5 (failed in year 2) → first-timers = 48. Answer 55 and 48.
Trap: Forgetting to subtract last year's failures (who reappear and are counted among this year's passes) gives 65 and 53 (option A).

q: The bar chart gives the batting averages of VK and RS for 11 calendar years from 2012 to 2022. Considering that 2015 and 2019 are world cup years, which one of the following options is true?
options: RS has a higher yearly batting average than that of VK in every world cup year.
VK has a higher yearly batting average than that of RS in every world cup year.
VK’s yearly batting average is consistently higher than that of RS between the two world cup years.
RS’s yearly batting average is consistently higher than that of VK in the last three years.
solution:
A: RS higher in both World-Cup years? 2015 yes (51 > 36) but 2019 no (VK 59.5 > RS 57.8) → false. B: VK higher in both? 2015 no → false. C: between the World-Cup years, i.e. 2016, 2017, 2018: VK 92 > 63, 76 > 72, 133 > 74 → true. D: RS higher in 2020–2022? 2021 VK 42 > RS 30 → false. Answer C.
Trap: 'Between the two world cup years' excludes the end years 2015 and 2019. The 2019 bars are deliberately close — read carefully.

q: The pie chart presents the percentage contribution of different macronutrients to a typical 2,000 kcal diet of a person. The typical energy density (kcal/g) of these macronutrients is given in the table: Carbohydrates 4, Proteins 4, Unsaturated fat 9, Saturated fat 9, Trans fat 9. The total fat (all three types), in grams, this person consumes is
solution:
Fat energy = (20 + 20 + 5)% of 2000 = 900 kcal. At 9 kcal per gram, fat = 900/9 = 100 g.
Trap: Option 3,600 comes from multiplying by 4 kcal/g instead of dividing; 44.4 from dividing 400 by 9. Convert % → kcal → grams.

q: The pie charts depict the shares of various power generation technologies in the total electricity generation of a country for the years 2007 and 2023. The renewable sources of electricity generation consist of Hydro, Solar and Wind. Assuming that the total electricity generated remains the same from 2007 to 2023, what is the percentage increase in the share of the renewable sources of electricity generation over this period?
solution:
Renewables 2007 = 30 + 5 + 5 = 40%; 2023 = 35 + 20 + 10 = 65%. Percentage increase = (65 − 40)/40 × 100 = 62.5%.
Trap: The increase is 25 percentage POINTS (option A) but 62.5 PERCENT. GATE loves points-vs-percent.

q: A certain country has 504 universities and 25951 colleges. These are categorised into Grades I, II, and III as shown in the given pie charts. What is the percentage, correct to one decimal place, of higher education institutions (colleges and universities) that fall into Grade III?
solution:
Grade III = 0.07 × 504 + 0.23 × 25951 = 35.28 + 5968.73 = 6004.0. Total = 26455. Share = 6004.0/26455 = 22.7%.
Trap: Averaging the two percentages (7 and 23 → 15.0, option C) ignores the very different sizes — always weight by counts.

q:
Details of prices of two items P and Q are presented in the table:
ItemCostProfit%Marked price
P5400–5860
Q–2510000

The ratio of cost of item P to cost of item Q is 3 : 4. Discount is calculated as the difference between the marked price and the selling price. The profit percentage is calculated as (Selling price − Cost)/Cost × 100. The discount on item Q, as a percentage of its marked price, is ____.
solution:
Cost Q = 5400 × 4/3 = 7200. Selling price Q = 7200 × 1.25 = 9000. Discount = 10000 − 9000 = 1000 = 10% of the marked price.
Trap: Item P's data (marked price 5860) is a distractor; only the cost ratio is needed from P.

q:
The table lists the top 5 nations according to the number of gold medals won in a tournament; also included are the number of silver and bronze medals won by them.
NationGoldSilverBronze
USA404441
Canada392724
Japan201213
Australia171916
France162622

Based only on the data provided in the table, which one of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: France will occupy the third place if the list were made on the basis of the total number of medals won.
The order of the top two nations will not change even if the list is made on the basis of the total number of medals won.
USA and Canada together have less than 50% of the medals awarded to the nations in the above table.
Canada has won twice as many total medals as Japan.
solution:
Totals: USA 125, Canada 90, Japan 45, Australia 52, France 64; all five = 376. A: by totals the order is USA, Canada, France → France third ✓. B: top two stay USA, Canada ✓. C: USA + Canada = 215 = 57.2% of 376 → 'less than 50%' is INCORRECT. D: Canada 90 = 2 × Japan 45 ✓. Answer C.
Trap: 'Which is INCORRECT' — evaluate all four; three are true.

q: The table lists the unit selling price of five products: P Rs. 100, Q Rs. 50, R Rs. 40, S Rs. 60, T Rs. 60. On a particular day, 250 items were sold with the average selling price of Rs. 60. The following observations were made: (i) The quantity of S sold was twice that of T. (ii) The quantity of R sold was thrice that of T. (iii) The quantity of Q sold was four times that of T. What is the quantity of product P sold on that day?
solution:
Let T = t, so S = 2t, R = 3t, Q = 4t, P = p. Count: p + 10t = 250. Revenue: 100p + 50(4t) + 40(3t) + 60(2t) + 60t = 250 × 60 = 15000 → 100p + 500t = 15000. Substituting p = 250 − 10t: 25000 − 500t = 15000 → t = 20, p = 50.
Trap: Average price × count = total revenue; set up two equations (count and revenue).
source: GATE 2026 ME · Q7 (also CE Set 2 Q7)

subtopic: other graphs / 2-D plots (combo charts, curves, function plots)
q: The number of units of a product sold in three different years and the respective net profits are presented in the figure. The cost/unit in year 3 was Rs. 1, which was half the cost/unit in year 2. The cost/unit in year 3 was one-third of the cost/unit in year 1. Taxes were paid on the selling price at 10%, 13% and 15% respectively for the three years. Net profit is calculated as the difference between the selling price and the sum of cost and taxes paid in that year. The ratio of the selling price in Year 2 to the selling price in Year 3 is ____.
solution:
Cost per unit: year 3 = 1, year 2 = 2, year 1 = 3. Net profit = SP − cost − tax = SP(1 − t) − cost ⇒ SP = (profit + cost)/(1 − t). Year 2: (296 + 400)/0.87 = 800. Year 3: (210 + 300)/0.85 = 600. Ratio 800 : 600 = 4 : 3.
Trap: Tax is on SELLING price, so divide by (1 − t), don't add t% of cost. 'Half the cost/unit in year 2' means year-2 cost = 2.

subtopic: other graphs / 2-D plots (combo charts, curves, function plots)
q: The chart below shows the data of the number of cars bought by Millennials and Gen X people in a country from the year 2010 to 2020 as well as the yearly fuel consumption of the country (in Million liters). Considering the data presented in the chart, which one of the following options is true?
options: The percentage increase in fuel consumption from 2010 to 2015 is more than the percentage increase in fuel consumption from 2015 to 2020.
The increase in the number of Millennial car buyers from 2015 to 2020 is less than the decrease in the number of Gen X car buyers from 2010 to 2015.
The increase in the number of Millennial car buyers from 2010 to 2015 is more than the decrease in the number of Gen X car buyers from 2010 to 2015.
The decrease in the number of Gen X car buyers from 2015 to 2020 is more than the increase in the number of Millennial car buyers from 2010 to 2015.
solution:
A: fuel growth 2010→15 = 20%, 2015→20 = 50% → false. B: Millennial increase 2015→20 = 15,000 vs Gen X decrease 2010→15 = 10,000; 15,000 < 10,000 false. C: Millennial increase 2010→15 = 25,000 > Gen X decrease 2010→15 = 10,000 → TRUE. D: Gen X decrease 2015→20 = 5,000 > 25,000 false. Answer C.
Trap: Two y-axes: read the bars on the right axis (thousands of people) and the line on the left axis. Percentage change vs absolute change in option A.

subtopic: other graphs / 2-D plots (combo charts, curves, function plots)
q: The plot below shows the relationship between the mortality risk of cardiovascular disease and the number of steps a person walks per day. Based on the data, which one of the following options is true?
options: The risk reduction on increasing the steps/day from 0 to 10000 is less than the risk reduction on increasing the steps/day from 10000 to 20000.
The risk reduction on increasing the steps/day from 0 to 5000 is less than the risk reduction on increasing the steps/day from 15000 to 20000.
For any 5000 increment in steps/day the largest risk reduction occurs on going from 0 to 5000.
For any 5000 increment in steps/day the largest risk reduction occurs on going from 15000 to 20000.
solution:
Risk reductions per 5000-step block: 0→5k ≈ 0.55, 5k→10k ≈ 0.27, 10k→15k ≈ 0.09, 15k→20k ≈ 0.05. A (0→10k reduction 0.82 < 10k→20k reduction 0.14) false; B false; C: largest drop is 0→5000 → TRUE; D false.
Trap: A convex decreasing curve = diminishing returns: equal x-steps give shrinking drops. Read slopes, not levels.

subtopic: other graphs / 2-D plots (combo charts, curves, function plots)
q: For positive real numbers S and K, the function $H_{K}$(S) is defined as $H_{K}$(S) = max(S − K, 0), where max(a, b) = a if a > b and b if a ≤ b. The graph shows the plot of a function N(S) versus S. N(S) can be expressed as ____.
solution:
$H_{10}$(S) is 0 until S = 10, then rises with slope 1. To stop the rise at S = 20, subtract a second ramp starting at 20: $H_{10}$(S) − $H_{20}$(S) = (S−10) − (S−20) = 10 for S ≥ 20. Check: S = 15 → 5 − 0 = 5 ✓; S = 25 → 15 − 5 = 10 ✓. Option A. (B would slope down after 20; C is negative; D starts at 15.)
Trap: Building piecewise graphs from 'hinge' (ReLU-like) functions — a pattern familiar to DA students: each kink = add/subtract a hinge with the change in slope.

q: According to the map shown in the figure, which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The library is located to the northwest of the canteen.
The hospital is located to the east of the chemistry lab.
The chemistry lab is to the southeast of physics lab.
The classrooms and canteen are next to each other.
solution:
A: Library vs Canteen — same row, Library is due WEST, not north-west → false. B: Hospital is NORTH of the chemistry lab, not east → false. C: Chemistry lab is south (other side of the cross road) and east (other side of the main road) of the Physics lab → south-east ✓. D: Classrooms (SW) and Canteen (NE) are diagonally opposite → false.
Trap: Directions are relative to the reference object named second ('X is to the SE of Y' means stand at Y).

q: The diagram shows a river system consisting of 7 segments, marked P, Q, R, S, T, U and V. It splits the land into 5 zones, marked Z1, Z2, Z3, Z4 and Z5. We need to connect these zones using the least number of bridges. Out of the following options, which one is correct?
solution:
Treat zones as nodes and a bridge on a segment as an edge between the two zones it separates. Connecting 5 zones needs at least 4 bridges (a spanning tree). A (P, Q, T) has only 3 edges and leaves Z4 isolated. B (P, Q, S, T) contains the cycle Z1–Z3–Z5 and still misses Z4. C (Q, R, T, V) = Z1–Z3, Z2–Z3, Z5–Z3, Z4–Z3 → all connected with 4 bridges ✓. D uses 5 (not least).
Trap: Minimum connections for n regions = n − 1 (spanning tree); also check that no option 'wastes' a bridge on a cycle.

q: Four cities P, Q, R and S are connected through one-way routes as shown in the figure. The travel time between any two connected cities is one hour. The boxes beside each city name describe the starting time of first train of the day and their frequency of operation. For example, from city P, the first trains of the day start at 8 AM with a frequency of 90 minutes to each of R and S. A person does not spend additional time at any city other than the waiting time for the next connecting train. If the person starts from R at 7 AM and is required to visit S and return to R, what is the minimum time required?
solution:
From R the only route is R→Q: leave 7:00, reach Q 8:00. Q's trains: 5, 7, 9, … → leave 9:00, reach P 10:00. P's trains: 8:00, 9:30, 11:00 → leave 11:00, reach S 12:00. S's trains: 8:00 + 45k → 12:30 departure, reach R 1:30 PM. Total 6 h 30 min. (Every other route to S also passes through Q and P, so this is minimal.)
Trap: Waiting times dominate — list the departure times at each city instead of adding travel hours only.

q:
The number of student in three classes is in the ratio 3 : 13 : 6. If 18 students are added to each class, the ratio changes to 15 : 35 : 21.
The total number of students in all the three classes in the beginning was :
solution:
Let the classes be 3k, 13k, 6k. (3k + 18)/(13k + 18) = 15/35 → 105k + 630 = 195k + 270 → k = 4 (check third: (12 + 18)/(24 + 18) = 30/42 = 15/21 ✓). Total = 22k = 88.
Trap: Adding the same number to every term changes the ratio — never add 18 to the ratio numbers directly.

q: The ratio of the number of girls to boys in class VIII is the same as the ratio of the number of boys to girls in class IX. The total number of students (boys and girls) in classes VIII and IX is 450 and 360, respectively. If the number of girls in classes VIII and IX is the same, then the number of girls in each class is
solution:
Let g = girls in each class. Class VIII: g girls, 450 − g boys; class IX: g girls, 360 − g boys. Given g/(450 − g) = (360 − g)/g → g² = (450 − g)(360 − g) = 162000 − 810g + g² → g = 200.
Trap: 'Ratio of girls to boys in VIII equals ratio of boys to girls in IX' — write the cross-ratio carefully; check: 200:250 = 160:200 = 4:5 ✓.

q: A person sold two different items at the same price. He made 10% profit in one item, and 10% loss in the other item. In selling these two items, the person made a total of
solution:
Let each selling price = 100. Cost of item 1 = 100/1.1 = 90.91; cost of item 2 = 100/0.9 = 111.11; total cost 202.02 vs revenue 200 → loss 2.02/202.02 = 1%. Shortcut: equal selling prices with ±x% always give a loss of x²/100 % = 1%.
Trap: Same SELLING price ⇒ loss of (x/10)²%; same COST price ⇒ no profit no loss. Students who average +10 and −10 get 0.

q: A shopkeeper buys shirts from a producer and sells them at 20% profit. A customer has to pay ₹3,186.00 including 18% taxes, per shirt. At what price did the shopkeeper buy each shirt from the producer?
solution:
Customer pays 3186 including 18% tax → shopkeeper's selling price = 3186/1.18 = 2700. That is 120% of his cost → cost = 2700/1.2 = 2250.
Trap: Remove the tax first (divide by 1.18), then the profit (divide by 1.2). Subtracting percentages (3186 × 0.62) gives a wrong answer.

q: Which one of the following numbers is exactly divisible by ($11^{13}+1$)?
solution:
Let a = 11¹³. Then a + 1 divides a² − 1 = (a − 1)(a + 1), hence also divides (a² − 1)(a² + 1) = a⁴ − 1 = 11⁵² − 1. (General rule: xⁿ + 1 divides x²ⁿ − 1, and x²ⁿ − 1 divides $x^{2nk}$ − 1.)
Trap: 11²⁶ + 1 = a² + 1 is NOT divisible by a + 1 (remainder 2). Use a = 11¹³ substitution to see the algebra.

q: the digit in the unit's place of the product $3^{999}\times 7^{1000}$ is __________.
solution:
Unit digits cycle with period 4: 3 → 3, 9, 7, 1; 7 → 7, 9, 3, 1. 999 = 4·249 + 3 → 3⁹⁹⁹ ends in 7. 1000 = 4·250 → 7¹⁰⁰⁰ ends in 1. Product ends in 7 × 1 = 7.
Trap: Use exponent mod 4 (remainder 0 means the 4th term of the cycle, not the 0th).

q:
For positive non-zero real variables p and q, if
log(p² + q²) = log p + log q + 2 log 3,
then, the value of (p⁴ + q⁴)/(p²q²) is
solution:
log(p² + q²) = log(pq·9) ⇒ p² + q² = 9pq. Divide by pq: p/q + q/p = 9. Required (p⁴ + q⁴)/(p²q²) = (p/q)² + (q/p)² = (p/q + q/p)² − 2 = 81 − 2 = 79.
Trap: 81 (option B) forgets the −2 from squaring a sum.

q: For a real number x > 1,$$\frac{1}{\log_2 x}+\frac{1}{\log_3 x}+\frac{1}{\log_4 x}=1$$The value of x is
solution:
1/$\log_{b}$ x = $\log_{x}$ b. So $\log_{x}$ 2 + $\log_{x}$ 3 + $\log_{x}$ 4 = $\log_{x}$ 24 = 1 ⇒ x = 24.
Trap: The reciprocal-base identity 1/$\log_{b}$ x = $\log_{x}$ b turns a sum of reciprocals into one logarithm of a product.

q: A shop has 4 distinct flavors of ice-cream. One can purchase any number of scoops of any flavor. The order in which the scoops are purchased is inconsequential. If one wants to purchase 3 scoops of ice-cream, in how many ways can one make that purchase?
solution:
Unordered selection of 3 scoops from 4 flavours with repetition allowed = combinations with repetition C(n + r − 1, r) = C(6, 3) = 20. (Cases: all three same 4, two same + one different 4×3 = 12, all different C(4,3) = 4; total 20.)
Trap: 24 = 4P3 ignores repeated flavours and wrongly counts order; 4³ = 64 counts order.

q: Three husband-wife pairs are to be seated at a circular table that has six identical chairs. Seating arrangements are defined only by the relative position of the people. How many seating arrangements are possible such that every husband sits next to his wife?
solution:
Glue each couple into a block: 3 blocks round a table → (3 − 1)! = 2 arrangements; each couple can sit in 2 orders → 2³ = 8. Total 2 × 8 = 16.
Trap: Circular arrangements: fix one block to remove rotations ((n−1)!), then multiply internal arrangements.

q:
Three distinct sets of indistinguishable twins are to be seated at a circular table that has 8 identical chairs. Unique seating arrangements are defined by the relative positions of the people.
How many unique seating arrangements are possible such that each person is sitting next to their twin?
solution:
Twins (indistinguishable within a pair) must sit together, so each pair is a block of 2; with 2 empty chairs the circle holds 3 blocks AA, BB, CC and 2 single empty seats E, E. Up to rotation: fix block AA; arrange BB, CC, E, E in the remaining linear order: 4!/(2!) = 12 (the two E's are identical; the blocks' internal order doesn't matter because twins are indistinguishable).
Trap: Indistinguishable twins → no ×2 per pair; identical empty chairs → divide by 2!.

q: A series of natural numbers F₁, F₂, F₃, F₄, F₅, F₆, F₇, … obeys F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n−1) for all integers n ≥ 2. If F₆ = 37 and F₇ = 60, then what is F₁?
solution:
Run the recurrence backwards: F₅ = F₇ − F₆ = 23, F₄ = 37 − 23 = 14, F₃ = 23 − 14 = 9, F₂ = 14 − 9 = 5, F₁ = 9 − 5 = 4. Series 4, 5, 9, 14, 23, 37, 60.
Trap: Work backwards with subtraction: F(n−1) = F(n+1) − F(n).

q:
Which one of the given options is a possible value of x in the following sequence?
3, 7, 15, x, 63, 127, 255
solution:
3, 7, 15, x, 63, 127, 255 = 2² − 1, 2³ − 1, 2⁴ − 1, …, 2⁸ − 1 (equivalently each term = 2 × previous + 1). x = 2⁵ − 1 = 31.
Trap: Check the rule on ALL given terms (63 = 2·31 + 1 confirms).

q: A surveyor has to measure the horizontal distance from her position to a distant reference point C. Using her position as the center, a 200 m horizontal line segment is drawn with the two endpoints A and B. Points A, B, and C are not collinear. Each of the angles ∠CAB and ∠CBA are measured as 87.8°. The distance (in m) of the reference point C from her position is nearest to
solution:
A, B are 100 m on either side of her (the centre of AB); ∠CAB = ∠CBA = 87.8° ⇒ C lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Distance = 100 × tan 87.8°. tan 87.8° = cot 2.2° ≈ 1/(2.2 × π/180) ≈ 26.04 → about 2604 m; precisely 100 × 26.03 = 2603 m.
Trap: Small-angle estimation: cot θ ≈ 1/θ (θ in radians) gives the answer in seconds; options 2603 vs 2606 then need the exact tan value — choose the nearest.

q: In the diagram, the lines QR and ST are parallel to each other (S on PQ, T on PR). The shortest distance between these two lines is half the shortest distance between the point P and line QR. What is the ratio of the area of the triangle PST to the area of the trapezium SQRT?
solution:
If P is at height h above QR and ST is h/2 above QR, then P is h/2 above ST: triangle PST is similar to PQR with ratio 1/2 → area ratio 1/4. Trapezium = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4 of PQR. Ratio = (1/4)/(3/4) = 1/3.
Trap: Areas of similar figures scale with the SQUARE of the length ratio; 1/2 (option D) is the length ratio, not the area ratio.

q: Corners are cut from an equilateral triangle to produce a regular convex hexagon as shown in the figure. The ratio of the area of the regular convex hexagon to the area of the original equilateral triangle is
solution:
For a regular hexagon the cuts must trisect each side: the triangle has side 3a and area ∝ 9a²; each corner triangle has side a and area ∝ a². Hexagon = 9 − 3 = 6 units → ratio 6/9 = 2 : 3.
Trap: A regular hexagon needs equal sides, which forces the corner triangles to have side 1/3 of the big side.

q: Four identical cylindrical chalk-sticks, each of radius r = 0.5 cm and length l = 10 cm, are bound tightly together using a duct tape as shown in the figure. The width of the duct tape is equal to the length of the chalk-stick. The area (in cm²) of the duct tape required to wrap the bundle of chalk-sticks once, is
solution:
Tight band around equal touching circles = sum of straight segments + one full circumference: straight parts = 4 × (distance between neighbouring centres) = 4 × 2r = 4; arcs = 4 quarter circles = 2πr = π. Tape length = 4 + π; area = 10(4 + π) cm².
Trap: The arcs always add up to exactly ONE full circle (total turning 360°), however many sticks there are.

q: The city of Atlantis was made of alternating concentric circular rings of land (shaded) and water (not shaded). The radius of Inner Island was 2.5 stades. The water surrounding Inner Island was one stade wide (length AB). This was surrounded by two pairs of alternating rings of land and water. The first pair of land and water was two stades wide each (lengths BC and CD), and the outer pair is three stades wide each (lengths DE and EF). The ratio of the surface area of the land to that of the water in the city of Atlantis is ____ (round off to two decimal places).
solution:
Areas ∝ r² differences. Land = 2.5² + (5.5² − 3.5²) + (10.5² − 7.5²) = 6.25 + 18 + 54 = 78.25. Water = (3.5² − 2.5²) + (7.5² − 5.5²) + (13.5² − 10.5²) = 6 + 26 + 72 = 104. Ratio = 0.752 ≈ 0.75.
Trap: Ring area = π(R² − r²), not π(R − r)²; π cancels in the ratio.

q: A square with sides of length 6 cm is given. The boundary of the shaded region is defined by two semi-circles whose diameters are the sides of the square, as shown. The area of the shaded region is ____ cm².
solution:
Each semicircle = 9π/2. Overlap (lens) = 2 × (quarter circle − right triangle) = 2 × (9π/4 − 9/2) = 9π/2 − 9. Shaded = 9π/2 + 9π/2 − 2(9π/2 − 9) = 18 cm².
Trap: Symmetric difference: subtract the overlap TWICE (once from each semicircle). The π terms cancel — a common GATE design.

q: In the triangle PQR, the lengths of PT and TR are in the ratio of 3 : 2. ST is parallel to QR. Two semi-circles are drawn with PS and PQ as diameters, as shown in the figure. Which one of the following statements is true about the shaded area PQS?
options: The shaded area is $\frac{16}{9}$ times the area of the semi-circle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is equal to the area of the semi-circle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is $\frac{14}{9}$ times the area of the semi-circle with the diameter PS.
The shaded area is $\frac{14}{25}$ times the area of the semi-circle with the diameter PQ.
solution:
ST ∥ QR ⇒ PS/PQ = PT/PR = 3/5. Semicircle areas ∝ diameter²: PQ ↔ 25, PS ↔ 9. Shaded = 25 − 9 = 16 units = (16/9) × semicircle(PS). (It is 16/25 of the PQ semicircle, not 14/25.)
Trap: Basic proportionality theorem gives the side ratio 3 : 5 (not 3 : 2).

q:
Consider the following sample of numbers:
9, 18, 11, 14, 15, 17, 10, 69, 11, 13
The median of the sample is
solution:
Sort: 9, 10, 11, 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 18, 69. Even count (10) → median = average of 5th and 6th = (13 + 14)/2 = 13.5.
Trap: The outlier 69 affects the mean (18.7, option D) but not the median.

q: The frequency chart shows the frequency distribution of marks obtained by a set of students in an exam. From the data presented, which one of the following is CORRECT?
solution:
Mode = 7 (frequency 14). Median: n = 50, the 25th and 26th values; cumulative 3, 12, 23, 30 → both are 6 → median 6. Mean = (9 + 36 + 55 + 42 + 98 + 16 + 36)/50 = 292/50 = 5.84. So mode > median > mean.
Trap: Median from a frequency table: use cumulative frequencies, not the middle bar.

q: Which one of the options can be inferred about the mean, median, and mode for the given probability distribution (probability mass function) P(x) of a variable x?
solution:
The pmf is symmetric about 0 ⇒ mean = 0 and median = 0. It is bimodal with the highest bars at x = ±13 ⇒ mode ≠ 0. So mean = median ≠ mode.
Trap: Symmetry gives mean = median immediately; mode is where the peak is, which for a bimodal distribution is away from the centre.

q:
There are five bags each containing identical sets of ten distinct chocolates. One chocolate is picked from each bag.
The probability that at least two chocolates are identical is ________.
solution:
Each bag gives one of 10 chocolates; all-different outcomes = 10·9·8·7·6 = 30240 of 10⁵. P(all different) = 0.3024 ⇒ P(at least two identical) = 1 − 0.3024 = 0.6976.
Trap: This is the birthday problem; 'at least two' ⇒ use the complement.

q:
A box contains five balls of same size and shape. Three of them are green coloured balls and two of them are orange coloured balls. Balls are drawn from the box one at a time. If a green ball is drawn, it is not replaced. If an orange ball is drawn, it is replaced with another orange ball.
First ball is drawn. What is the probability of getting an orange ball in the next draw?
solution:
First draw green (3/5): no replacement → 2 G, 2 O left → P(orange next) = 2/4. First draw orange (2/5): replaced → still 3 G, 2 O → 2/5. Total = (3/5)(1/2) + (2/5)(2/5) = 3/10 + 4/25 = 23/50.
Trap: Total probability over the first draw; replacement rules differ by colour.

q: An unbiased six-faced dice whose faces are marked with numbers 1,2,3,4,5, and 6 is rolled twice in succession and the number on the top face is recorded each time. The probability that the number appearing in the second roll is an integer multiple of the number appearing in the first roll is ____
solution:
Count pairs (a, b) with b a multiple of a: a = 1 → 6, a = 2 → {2, 4, 6} 3, a = 3 → {3, 6} 2, a = 4, 5, 6 → 1 each. Total 14/36 = 7/18.
Trap: Every number is a multiple of itself (1 × a), so (a, a) counts.

q: A final year student appears for placement interview in two companies, S and T. Based on her interview performance, she estimates the probability of receiving job offers from companies S and T to be 0.8 and 0.6 , respectively. Let p be the probability that she receives job offers from both the companies. Select the most appropriate option.
solution:
P(S ∩ T) ≥ P(S) + P(T) − 1 = 0.4 (since P(S ∪ T) ≤ 1) and P(S ∩ T) ≤ min(P(S), P(T)) = 0.6. So 0.4 ≤ p ≤ 0.6. (If independent, p = 0.48 — inside the range.)
Trap: Without independence you can only bound the intersection (Fréchet bounds); don't multiply.

q:
Given below are two statements and two conclusions.
Statement 1 : All purple are green
Statement 2 : All black are green
Conclusion I : Some black are purple.
Conclusion II : No black is purple
Based on the above statements and conclusions, which one of the following options is logically CORRECT?
options: Both conclusion I and II are correct.
Either conclusion I or II is correct.
solution:
Both purple and black are inside green, but nothing relates purple to black. In a Venn diagram black may overlap purple (then I true, II false) or be disjoint from it (I false, II true). Neither is certain on its own, but exactly one of them must hold: 'Some black are purple' and 'No black is purple' are contradictory (a complementary pair about the same two terms). Hence 'Either conclusion I or II is correct'.
Trap: 'Either–or' is the answer only when the two conclusions are an exact complementary pair (Some/No or All/Some-not with the SAME subject and predicate) and neither follows individually.

q:
Given below are two statements and four conclusions drawn based on the statements.
Statement I : Some bottles are cups.
Statement II : All cups are knives.
Conclusion I : Some bottles are knives.
Conclusion II : Some knives are cups.
Conclusion III : All cups are bottles.
Conclusion IV : All knives are cups.
Which one of the following options can be logically inferred?
options: Only conclusion I and conclusion II are correct.
Only conclusion II and conclusion III are correct.
Only conclusion II and conclusion IV are correct.
Only conclusion III and conclusion IV are correct.
solution:
Some bottles are cups + all cups are knives ⇒ those bottle-cups are knives ⇒ some bottles are knives (I ✓). 'All cups are knives' (with cups existing) ⇒ some knives are cups (II ✓, conversion). III (all cups are bottles) and IV (all knives are cups) do not follow — draw cups as a small circle inside knives, partly overlapping bottles.
Trap: 'All A are B' converts only to 'Some B are A', never to 'All B are A' (IV is the conversion trap).

q:
Given below are two statements and four conclusions drawn based on the statements.
Statement 1 : Some soaps are clean.
Statement 2 : All clean objects are wet.
Conclusion I : Some clean objects are soaps.
Conclusion II : No clean object is a soap.
Conclusion III : Some wet objects are soaps.
Conclusion IV : All wet objects are soaps.
Which one of the following options can be logically inferred?
options: Either conclusion I or conclusion II is correct
Either conclusion III or conclusion IV is correct
Only conclusion I and conclusion III are correct
solution:
Some soaps are clean ⇒ some clean objects are soaps (I ✓, an I-statement converts simply). Those clean soaps are wet (all clean objects are wet) ⇒ some wet objects are soaps (III ✓). II contradicts the first statement; IV (all wet are soaps) does not follow.
Trap: Here I and II are a complementary pair, but since I definitely follows, the answer is NOT 'either I or II'.

subtopic: deduction: conditionals and negation of quantified statements
q: 'When the teacher is in the room, all students stand silently.' If the above statement is true, which one of the following statements is not necessarily true?
options: If any student is not standing silently, then the teacher is not in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are silent.
If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room.
When the teacher is in the room, all students are standing.
solution:
Statement: Teacher-in ⇒ (standing AND silent). A is the contrapositive (if some student is not standing silently ⇒ teacher not in room) — always true. B and D keep only part of the consequent — true. C 'If all students are standing, then the teacher is in the room' is the CONVERSE — not necessarily true (students may stand while the teacher is away).
Trap: Contrapositive ≡ original; converse and inverse are NOT implied. Weakening the 'then' part (dropping 'silently') keeps truth.

subtopic: deduction: conditionals and negation of quantified statements
q: 'When it is raining, peacocks dance.' Based only on this sentence, which one of the following options is necessarily true?
options: Peacocks dance only when it is raining.
When peacocks dance, it is raining.
When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining.
When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance.
solution:
Rain ⇒ Dance. Contrapositive: not Dance ⇒ not Rain — 'When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining' (C) is necessarily true. A ('only when raining') and B (Dance ⇒ Rain) are the converse; D (no rain ⇒ no dance) is the inverse — neither follows.
Trap: 'Only when' reverses the arrow: 'P only if Q' means P ⇒ Q.

subtopic: deduction: conditionals and negation of quantified statements
q: 'All the mangoes in the basket are good.' If the above statement is false, then which one of the following statements is necessarily true?
options: All the mangoes in the basket are not good.
No mango in the basket is good.
In the basket, some of the mangoes are good and some are not good.
There exists at least one mango in the basket that is not good.
solution:
The negation of 'All are good' is 'At least one is NOT good' (D). It does not say none are good (A/B), nor that some ARE good (C) — all of them could be bad.
Trap: ¬(∀x good) = ∃x ¬good. 'All … are not' (option A) is ambiguous English and is not the negation.
source: GATE 2026 ME · Q4 (also CE Set 2 Q4)

q: Consider a linear arrangement of seven bulbs, each of which can be in the ON or OFF states. The initial configuration of the bulbs is shown in the figure. In every Step, the states of the bulbs are changed based on the following rules: Any OFF bulb with exactly one ON neighbor at the end of the previous Step is turned ON. Any ON bulb with both neighbors ON at the end of the previous Step is turned OFF. The state of any bulb not meeting the conditions above is left unchanged. The states of bulbs at the end of Step 1 and Step 2 are also shown in the figure. The number of bulbs which are ON at the end of Step 8 is ____.
solution:
Apply the rules (end bulbs have one neighbour): Step 3: 1110111; Step 4: 1010101; Step 5: 1010101 — a fixed point (every OFF bulb now has two ON neighbours, every ON bulb has at most one ON neighbour). So from Step 4 onwards 4 bulbs are ON; at Step 8 → 4.
Trap: Look for a steady state instead of grinding 8 steps; and check your rule application against the given Steps 1–2 first.
source: GATE 2026 EE · Q9 (also CE Set 1 Q9)

q: The figures show three curves generated using an iterative algorithm. The total length of the curve generated after 'Iteration n' is:
solution:
Each iteration replaces every segment by 5 segments of 1/3 its length, multiplying the total length by 5/3. Iteration 1: 5/3; iteration 2: 25/9 = (5/3)²; so after n iterations, length = (5/3)ⁿ.
Trap: Count segments × segment length at the first two iterations, then generalise (a fractal like the Koch curve).

q:
________ is to surgery as writer is to ________
Which one of the following options maintains a similar logical relation in the above sentence?
solution:
A doctor performs surgery; a writer produces a book — person : what that person does/produces. 'Doctor, book' keeps the relation in both blanks.
Trap: Two-blank analogies: test each option in BOTH positions; 'Hospital, library' are places, not agents.

q:
Water: P:: Food: Q
Choose the P and Q combination from the options below to form a meaningful analogy.
solution:
Water quenches thirst; food satisfies hunger — 'Water : Thirst :: Food : Hunger' (thing : the need it removes). B mixes an action (drink) with a need; C uses a state of being full (satiated); D is unrelated.
Trap: Keep the SAME relation in both pairs and the same part of speech (noun need).

q:
Six students P, Q, R, S, T and U, with distinct heights, compare their heights and make the following observations:
Observation I : S is taller than R.
Observation II : Q is the shortest of all.
Observation III : U is taller than only one student.
Observation IV : T is taller than S but is not the tallest.
The number of students that are taller than R is the same as the number of students shorter than ________.
solution:
Ranks from shortest (1) to tallest (6): Q = 1 (shortest); U = 2 (taller than only one). The remaining ranks 3–6 go to P, R, S, T with R < S < T and T not the tallest ⇒ R = 3, S = 4, T = 5, P = 6. Students taller than R: S, T, P = 3. Students shorter than S: R, U, Q = 3. Answer S.
Trap: Turn each statement into a rank constraint; 'taller than only one' fixes rank 2.

q: Seven cars P, Q, R, S, T, U and V are parked in a row, not necessarily in that order. The cars T and U should be parked next to each other. The cars S and V also should be parked next to each other, whereas P and Q can't be parked next to each other. Q and S must be parked next to each other. R is parked to the immediate right of V. T is parked to the left of U. Based on the above statements, the only incorrect option given below is
options: There are two cars parked in between Q and V .
Q and R are not parked together.
V is the only car parked in between S and R .
Car P is parked at extreme end.
solution:
Q–S–V–R must be a consecutive block (Q next to S, S next to V, R immediately right of V; S cannot be between Q and V's other side). T–U is a block. P not next to Q. Valid rows: QSVRPTU, QSVRTUP, PTUQSVR, TUQSVRP. In every row exactly ONE car (S) is between Q and V, so A ('two cars between Q and V') is always false. B (Q and R not together) and C (V is the only car between S and R) are always true; D holds in 3 of 4 rows. The option that is incorrect in every arrangement is A.
Trap: 'Only incorrect' = the statement that can never be true. Build blocks first; D is only sometimes true, A is never true.

q: In a class of five students P, Q, R, S and T, only one student is known to have copied in the exam. The disciplinary committee recorded: P: 'R has copied in the exam.' Q: 'S has copied in the exam.' R: 'P did not copy in this exam.' S: 'Only one of us is telling the truth.' T: 'R is telling the truth.' The investigating team had authentic information that S never lies. Based on the information given above, the person who has copied in the exam is
solution:
S is truthful ⇒ exactly one statement (S's own) is true ⇒ P, Q, R, T all lie. R lies ⇒ 'P did not copy' is false ⇒ P copied. Check: P's claim (R copied) false ✓, Q's claim (S copied) false ✓, T's claim (R truthful) false ✓.
Trap: The truthful speaker's own statement counts among the 'one telling the truth'.

q:
Consider the relationships among P,Q,R,S, and T :
∙ P is the brother of Q.
∙ S is the daughter of Q.
∙ T is the sister of S.
∙ R is the mother of Q.
The following statements are made based on the relationships given above.
(1) R is the grandmother of S.
(2) P is the uncle of S and T.
(3)R has only one son.
(4) Q has only one daughter.
Which one of the following options is correct?
solution:
R is Q's mother and S is Q's daughter ⇒ R is S's grandmother (1 ✓). P is Q's brother, and S, T are Q's daughters ⇒ P is the uncle of S and T (2 ✓). (3) 'R has only one son' — P is a son of R; Q's gender is unknown, so this cannot be confirmed. (4) Q has two daughters (S and T) ⇒ false. Answer: both (1) and (2).
Trap: Gender of Q is never stated — don't assume. 'Sister of S' makes T a daughter of Q too.

q: Consider a five-digit number PQRST that has distinct digits P, Q, R, S and T, and satisfies the following conditions: P < Q; S > P > T; R < T. If integers 1 through 5 are used to construct such a number, the value of P is:
solution:
R < T < P, so at least two digits are smaller than P ⇒ P ≥ 3. Q > P and S > P, so at least two digits are larger than P ⇒ P ≤ 3. Hence P = 3 (R = 1, T = 2, {Q, S} = {4, 5}).
Trap: Count how many digits must be below and above P — no need to list numbers.

q: The Roman senator Meritorius, his brother, his son, and his daughter have varying oratory skill levels. They are seated in rows and columns as shown in the figure with exactly one person sitting in each box. It is known that (i) Meritorius' daughter and his brother are seated in the same column. (ii) His son is seated diagonally across the sibling of the worst orator. (iii) The best and worst orators are seated in the same row. Who is the best orator?
solution:
Siblings: Meritorius–brother and son–daughter. By (i) the daughter and the brother share a column, so the son and Meritorius share the other column. Worst = daughter is impossible (her sibling is the son himself, who cannot be diagonal to himself). Worst = brother: his sibling Meritorius must be diagonal to the son — but they are in the same column. Impossible. Worst = Meritorius: sibling = brother must be diagonal to the son, so the son is in the daughter's row and Meritorius in the brother's row; by (iii) the best is in Meritorius' row → the brother. Worst = son: sibling = daughter must be diagonal to the son, so the son is in the brother's row; by (iii) the best is in the son's row → the brother. Either way the best orator is Meritorius' brother.
Trap: Exhaust the small case space (4! seatings × 4! rankings); conditions (ii) and (iii) together pin the best orator even though seats are not unique.
source: GATE 2026 ME · Q9 (also CE Set 2 Q9)

q: If IMAGE and FIELD are coded as FHBNJ and EMFJG respectively then, which one among the given options is the most appropriate code for BEACH ?
solution:
IMAGE reversed is EGAMI; shift each letter +1 → FHBNJ ✓. FIELD reversed DLEIF → +1 → EMFJG ✓. BEACH reversed HCAEB → +1 → IDBFC.
Trap: When the code letters look scrambled, try reversing the word before applying a shift.

q: If HIDE and CAGE are coded as 19-23-7-11 and 5-2-17-11 respectively, then what is the code for HIGH ?
solution:
Each letter → the prime numbered by its alphabet position: H (8th) → 8th prime 19, I (9) → 23, D (4) → 7, E (5) → 11 ✓; C → 5, A → 2, G → 17 ✓. HIGH → 19-23-17-19.
Trap: Numbers that are all primes are a strong hint (2, 5, 7, 11, 17, 19, 23).

q: The minute-hand and second-hand of a clock cross each other _______ times between 09:15:00 AM and 09:45:00 AM on a day.
solution:
Relative speed: second hand 360°/min, minute hand 6°/min → second hand gains 354° per minute. At 09:15:00 the second hand (at 12) is 90° behind the minute hand (at 3). Crossings happen when the gain = 90° + 360°k. In 30 min the gain is 30 × 354 = 10620°, so k = 0, 1, …, 29 (90 + 360·29 = 10530 ≤ 10620) → 30 crossings.
Trap: Not exactly once per minute: in 30 minutes the second hand laps the minute hand 29.5 times; the starting offset decides 29 vs 30.

q: Rohit goes to a restaurant for lunch at about 1 PM . When he enters the restaurant, he notices that the hour and minute hands on the wall clock are exactly coinciding. After about an hour, when he leaves the restaurant, he notices that the clock hands are again exactly coinciding. How much time (in minutes) did Rohit spend at the restaurant?
solution:
Hour and minute hands coincide every 720/11 = 65 5/11 minutes (minute hand gains 5.5°/min, needs 360°). After 1 PM they coincide at 1:05 5/11, next at 2:10 10/11 → time spent 65 5/11 min.
Trap: Not 60 minutes — the hour hand moves on while the minute hand goes round.

q: In the 4 × 4 array shown, each cell of the first three rows has either a cross (X) or a number. The number in a cell represents the count of the immediate neighboring cells (left, right, top, bottom, diagonals) NOT having a cross (X). Given that the last row has no crosses (X), the sum of the four numbers to be filled in the last row is
solution:
Last-row cells and their non-X neighbours: (4,1): (3,1)=3 ✓, (3,2)=X, (4,2) ✓ → 2. (4,2): (3,1) ✓, (3,2) X, (3,3) ✓, (4,1) ✓, (4,3) ✓ → 4. (4,3): (3,2) X, (3,3) ✓, (3,4) X, (4,2) ✓, (4,4) ✓ → 3. (4,4): (3,3) ✓, (3,4) X, (4,3) ✓ → 2. Sum = 11.
Trap: Corner cells have only 3 neighbours, edge cells 5. (The given numbers in rows 1–3 also satisfy the rule — a good self-check.)

q: The symbols ○, ∗, Δ and □ are to be filled, one in each box. Rules: (1) every row and every column must contain each of the four symbols; (2) every 2 × 2 square delineated by bold lines must contain each of the four symbols. Which symbol will occupy the box marked with '?' in the partially filled figure?
solution:
Column 2 already has ○ (r2); the top-left block has ○; row 1 has Δ. Column 3 has ∗, □, Δ ⇒ r1c3 = ○. Then row 1 needs ∗ and □ in c1, c2. Column 1 already has ∗ (r4) ⇒ r1c1 = □, so '?' = ∗.
Trap: Sudoku-style: find the cell with the fewest possibilities first (r1c3 here).

q: The figure in Panel I is a grid of cells with four rows and four columns. The numbers on the top and on the left represent the number of cells that are to be shaded in that column and row, respectively. Which one of the options shown in Panel II represents the grid shaded correctly?
solution:
Check row 2 first (needs exactly 1): (i) and (iii) have 2 → out. (iv): row 3 has 1 (needs 2) → out. (ii): rows 3, 1, 2, 2 and columns 2, 2, 2, 2 ✓.
Trap: Check the most restrictive count (the row with 1) first to eliminate fast.

q: Which one of the following options best describes the transformation of the 2-dimensional figure P to Q, and then to R, as shown?
options:
Operation 1 : A clockwise rotation by 90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure
Operation 2 : A reflection along a horizontal line

Operation 1 : A counter clockwise rotation by 90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure
Operation 2 : A reflection along a vertical line

Operation 1 : A clockwise rotation by 90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure
Operation 2 : A reflection along a vertical line

Operation 1 : A counter clockwise rotation by 180° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure
Operation 2 : A reflection along a vertical line
solution:
Long arm of P points up-right (about +40°); in Q it points down-right (about −50°): a clockwise quarter turn. From Q to R the long arm flips from down-right to up-right while staying on the right side → reflection in a horizontal line. Checking all five tips (not just the long arm): rotate P by 90° clockwise → matches Q; reflect Q in a horizontal line → matches R. That is option A.
Trap: A single feature (the long arm) can be matched by several operation pairs; check a second, asymmetric feature (the other tips) before choosing between C (vertical reflection) and A.

q: Consider a square with the four corners P (top-left), Q (top-right), R (bottom-right), S (bottom-left) and the center T. Let X, Y and Z represent the following operations: X: rotation of the square by 180 degree with respect to the S-Q axis. Y: rotation of the square by 180 degree with respect to the P-R axis. Z: rotation of the square by 90 degree clockwise with respect to the axis perpendicular, going into the screen and passing through the point T. Consider the following three distinct sequences of operation (applied in the left to right order): (1) XYZZ (2) XY (3) ZZZZ. Which one of the following statements is correct as per the information provided above?
options: The sequence of operations (1) and (2) are equivalent
The sequence of operations (1) and (3) are equivalent
The sequence of operations (2) and (3) are equivalent
The sequence of operations (1), (2) and (3) are equivalent
solution:
A 180° flip about a diagonal acts on the corners like a reflection in that diagonal: X swaps P↔R (fixes S, Q); Y swaps Q↔S (fixes P, R). XY = reflection in one diagonal then in the perpendicular diagonal = rotation by 180° (and the square is flipped twice, so the same face is up). ZZ = 180°, ZZZZ = 360° = identity. So (1) XYZZ = 180° + 180° = identity = (3); (2) = 180° ≠ identity. Statement B.
Trap: Two reflections in perpendicular lines = a 180° rotation; four quarter-turns = identity.

q:
The given figure is reflected about the horizontal dashed line (drawn above the figure) and then rotated clockwise by 90° about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure. Which one of the following options correctly shows the resultant figure?
Options are labelled in the figure.
solution:
Track quadrants. Reflection in a horizontal line swaps top and bottom: bolt → BL, flag → BR, arrow → TL, crescent → TR. A 90° clockwise rotation then moves TL→TR, TR→BR, BR→BL, BL→TL: arrow → TR, crescent → BR, flag → BL, bolt → TL. The crescent's opening (facing right, +x) becomes, after the flip (still +x) and the rotation, facing down. That is option B. (Shortcut: reflect-in-horizontal then rotate-90°-cw = a single reflection in the diagonal from top-left to bottom-right, so the TL and BR objects stay in their corners.)
Trap: Use a corner-by-corner map and one asymmetric feature (the crescent's opening) instead of mentally rotating every shape.

q:
Examples of mirror and water reflections are shown in the figures. An object appears as the following image ('5:24' in seven-segment digits) after first reflecting in a mirror and then reflecting on water. The original object is
Options are labelled in the figure.
solution:
Mirror (left–right flip) followed by water (up–down flip) = rotation by 180°. So the object is the image rotated by 180°: the order of characters reverses and each character turns upside down. '5:24' → characters 4, 2, :, 5 each rotated: 4 → an upside-down 4 (looks like 'h'), 2 → 2, 5 → 5. Object = 'h2:5' with the colon between 2 and 5 → option A.
Trap: Two perpendicular reflections = 180° rotation (not a reflection). 2 and 5 are 180°-symmetric in seven-segment form, 4 is not.

q:
Consider a circle with its centre at the origin (O). Two operations are allowed on the circle. Operation 1: Scale independently along the x and y axes. Operation 2: Rotation in any direction about the origin. Which figure among the options can be achieved through a combination of these two operations on the given circle?
Options are labelled in the figure.
solution:
Both operations are linear maps fixing O, so any combination maps the circle to an ELLIPSE centred at O (possibly tilted). A ✓. B is an ellipse but moved away from O (needs a translation, not allowed). C and D are not ellipses — they are not symmetric about O (a linear image of a circle is always point-symmetric about O).
Trap: Scaling + rotation never translate and never create egg shapes; the result is always centrally symmetric.

subtopic: lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry
q: The least number of squares to be added in the figure to make AB a line of symmetry is
solution:
Reflection in AB maps row r ↔ row −1−r. Needed images: (1,−1)→(1,0) missing; (0,0)→(0,−1) missing; (1,1)→(1,−2) missing; (3,0)→(3,−1) missing; (4,0)→(4,−1) missing; (4,1)→(4,−2) missing. 6 squares must be added.
Trap: Read the figure carefully: the 'square' between the upper and lower squares in column 1 is an open gap, not a filled square — miscounting it gives 5.

subtopic: lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry
q: A line of symmetry is defined as a line that divides a figure into two parts in a way such that each part is a mirror image of the other part about that line. The figure consists of 20 unit squares arranged as shown (5 rows × 4 columns). In addition to the given black squares, up to 5 more may be coloured black. Which one among the following options depicts the minimum number of boxes that must be coloured black to achieve two lines of symmetry?
solution:
Two lines of symmetry here = the vertical centre line and the horizontal centre line (row 3). Row 4 is 'X i X X' — to be symmetric left–right, i must be black. Rows 2 and 4 must match (top–bottom symmetry): row 4 becomes X X X X, so row 2 must be X X X X → c and d black. Rows 1 and 5 already match (a X X b / j X X k). So colour c, d, i — 3 boxes.
Trap: Fix one axis at a time; changes for one axis can create new requirements for the other.

subtopic: lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry
q:
An object is said to have an n-fold rotational symmetry if the object, rotated by an angle of 2π/n, is identical to the original. Which one of the following objects exhibits 4-fold rotational symmetry about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the screen?
Options are labelled in the figure.
solution:
Rotate by 90° clockwise: the dot at the right corner of the top arm must move to the bottom corner of the right arm, then to the left corner of the bottom arm, then to the top corner of the left arm — a 'pinwheel'. Only B has exactly this pattern (all dots on the clockwise-leading corner).
Trap: Mirror-symmetric placements (like A, C, D) look balanced but are not rotationally symmetric; 4-fold rotation needs a consistent 'swirl'.

q:
A transparent square sheet shown is folded along the dotted line (the vertical centre line). The folded sheet will look like ____.
Options are labelled in the figure.
solution:
Folding the left half onto the right = reflecting the left drawing in the centre line (x → −x). The left curve becomes a curve from the peak down to the right edge at the same end-height as the right curve, so the two curves form a closed lens. The reflected curve drops steeply first, so it lies BELOW the right curve. Vertical ticks stay vertical under a left–right reflection and remain on the lower arc pointing up; the right curve's horizontal ticks are unchanged. That is option A.
Trap: Because the sheet is transparent, both halves stay visible; reflection preserves vertical/horizontal directions of the ticks but changes left/right positions.

q:
A square paper, shown in figure (I), is folded along the dotted lines as shown in the figures (II) and (III). Then a few cuts are made as shown in figure (IV). Which one of the following patterns will be obtained when the paper is unfolded?
Options are labelled in the figure.
solution:
Unfold fold 2 (reflect in y = x) then fold 1 (reflect in x + y = 2). Top-edge triangle → copies at the middle of the top, right, left and bottom edges, each with its apex at the edge (pointing outward). The right triangle with hypotenuse on fold 1 + its mirror image = an axis-aligned SQUARE near the top-left corner; reflecting in y = x places a second square near the bottom-right corner. The rectangle touching fold 2 + its mirror image = an L-shape near the top-right; fold 1 copies it to the bottom-left. Pattern = option A.
Trap: Reflecting in a 45° line turns a horizontal rectangle vertical — that is how the L-shapes appear. A right triangle with its hypotenuse on the fold doubles into a square (diamond only if the legs were at 45°).

q: A rectangular paper of 20 cm × 8 cm is folded 3 times. Each fold is made along the line of symmetry, which is perpendicular to its long edge. The perimeter of the final folded sheet (in cm) is
solution:
Each fold is along the line of symmetry perpendicular to the CURRENT long edge. 20 × 8 → fold the 20 side: 10 × 8 → long edge is now 10: 5 × 8 → long edge is now 8: 5 × 4. Perimeter = 2(5 + 4) = 18 cm.
Trap: After the first fold the long edge may change — halving 20 three times (2.5 × 8, perimeter 21 = option D) is the trap.

q:
Two identical sheets A and B, of dimensions 24 cm × 16 cm, can be folded into half using two distinct operations, FO1 or FO2.
In FO1, the axis of folding remains parallel to the initial long edge, and in FO2, the axis of folding remains parallel to the initial short edge.
If sheet A is folded twice using FO1, and sheet B is folded twice using FO2, the ratio of the perimeters of the final shapes of A and B is
solution:
FO1: axis parallel to the long edge (24) → halves the 16 side; twice → A becomes 24 × 4, perimeter 56. FO2: axis parallel to the short edge (16) → halves the 24 side; twice → B becomes 6 × 16, perimeter 44. Ratio 56 : 44 = 14 : 11.
Trap: A fold axis parallel to an edge halves the OTHER dimension.

subtopic: Assembling and grouping (tiling, cutting into pieces, matching parts)
q:
The figure shows two 4-tile patterns (a 2 × 2 square and a 1 × 4 straight bar). Either one or both of the patterns can be used any number of times and in any orientation to construct a new pattern. Which one of the options below cannot be constructed by using only these two 4-tile patterns assuming there are no overlaps among them?
Options are labelled in the figure.
solution:
Every piece has 4 tiles, so the target area must be a multiple of 4: 8, 12, 15, 20 → the 3 × 5 = 15 rectangle is impossible. (2 × 4 = two squares; 3 × 4 = three bars; 4 × 5 = five vertical bars.)
Trap: Area/divisibility check first — it decides before any trial tiling.

subtopic: Assembling and grouping (tiling, cutting into pieces, matching parts)
q: A black square PQRS has been cut into two parts. One part of it is shown in Panel I. Which one of the shapes in Panel II is the other part?
solution:
The missing part = the '.' cells: row 2 cols 2, 5, 6; row 3 cols 2–5; row 4 col 4; row 5 cols 2–4. Trimmed to its bounding box (cols 2–6): X..XX / XXXX. / ..X.. / XXX.. — exactly option (iii).
Trap: Compare row by row; (i), (ii) and (iv) differ in only one or two cells of the bottom rows.

subtopic: Assembling and grouping (tiling, cutting into pieces, matching parts)
q:
A cube is to be cut into 8 pieces of equal size and shape. Here, each cut should be straight and it should not stop till it reaches the other end of the cube.
The minimum number of such cuts required is
solution:
Three cuts through the centre parallel to the three pairs of faces cut the cube into 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 equal small cubes. Fewer is impossible: each straight, complete cut can at most double the number of pieces, so 2 cuts give at most 4.
Trap: Count pieces after each cut: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8.
